```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Finite mixture models represent population heterogeneity as a small number
of unobserved subpopulations, the latent classes, each characterized by its
own distribution of the observed indicators (McLachlan and Peel, 2000). In
latent profile analysis the class-specific parameters are the means and
variances of continuous indicators; in latent class analysis they are the
response probabilities of categorical indicators. When observations are
nested within higher-level units, the units may themselves differ in the
distribution of classes. In the data used here, course enrolments are nested
within students, and students differ in the proportion of their enrolments
that show a given pattern of engagement. The two-level mixture model of
Vermunt (2003) represents this variation with a second, higher-level latent
variable whose categories, the group classes, are defined by their
distributions over the lower-level profiles. For a fixed number of classes,
estimation yields the class sizes and the class-specific parameters. The
number of classes, however, is not a parameter of the model: it is specified
before estimation, at both levels in a two-level model, and every subsequent
inference is conditional on that specification.

Determining the number of classes is difficult because each conventional
criterion for model comparison is deficient in a specific respect. The
maximized likelihood is non-decreasing in the number of classes, since a
model with k + 1 classes contains the model with k classes as a special
case. The likelihood ratio test of k against k + 1 classes does not have its
usual chi-square reference distribution, because the null hypothesis places
a mixing proportion on the boundary of the parameter space and leaves the
parameters of the omitted class unidentified (McLachlan and Peel, 2000).
Valid p-values can be obtained by parametric bootstrap (McLachlan, 1987), at
the cost of refitting both models to many simulated data sets. Information
criteria avoid hypothesis testing by penalizing the deviance for the number
of estimated parameters; criteria with a weaker penalty, such as the Akaike
information criterion, select more classes than criteria with a stronger
penalty, such as the Bayesian information criterion (Nylund, Asparouhov and
Muthén, 2007).

Applied data introduce further complications. In large samples the Bayesian
information criterion frequently continues to decrease as classes are added,
because minor misspecifications become detectable and each additional class
absorbs part of them. The minimum then falls at the largest model fitted,
and the magnitude of successive improvements is more informative than the
location of the minimum. In a two-level model the numbers of lower- and
higher-level classes must be determined jointly, and the penalty of the
Bayesian information criterion depends on whether the sample size is taken
as the number of higher-level units or of lower-level observations
(Lukočienė, Varriale and Vermunt, 2010). Moreover, a model may fit well yet
separate its classes poorly, and the reported solution may be a local rather
than the global maximum of the likelihood.

This article applies class enumeration to a two-level latent profile model.
All combinations of the specified numbers of profiles and group classes are
estimated with `enumerate_classes()`, and every fitted model is retained.
Each candidate is characterized by its information criteria under both
definitions of the sample size, by the change in a criterion with each
additional profile and group class, by the knee of each resulting curve, by
the certainty of its classification and by diagnostics of its estimation.
Selected candidates are then compared directly, and the chosen candidate is
extracted for substantive analysis.

The full evidence is reported because no single statistic determines the
number of classes. Considered jointly, the criteria, the changes between
neighbouring candidates and the indices of classification quality indicate
where additional classes cease to improve the model, and a decision based on
them can be stated, justified and reproduced from the reported tables.
[Model selection](model-selection.html) defines each source of evidence and
discusses its interpretation and limitations.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_enrolments <- nrow(course_engagement)
n_students <- with(course_engagement, length(unique(student)))
```

## Data

The examples use `course_engagement`, a long-format data frame with one row
per course enrolment, comprising
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments of `r n_students`
students. Five measures of course activity serve as indicators: browsing of
the course site, lecture viewing, forum reading, forum posting and
attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course, so that zero
denotes the course mean. The column `student` identifies the student to whom
each enrolment belongs.

```{r data}
head(course_engagement)
```

Because enrolments are nested within students, the profiles describe
patterns of activity within a single course, and the group classes describe
students by the distribution of their enrolments over those patterns.

## Fitting the candidate models

`enumerate_classes()` takes the data, the indicators (`vars`) and the group
identifier (`id`). The arguments `n_profiles` and `n_group_classes` specify
the numbers of classes to be considered, and one model is estimated for each
combination; here the number of profiles ranges from one to six and the
number of group classes from one to four. The argument `model` specifies the
within-profile covariance structure. `"VVI"` assigns each profile its own
variances and constrains the covariances to zero; when `model` is omitted,
the four basic structures are estimated for every combination.

The likelihood of a mixture model is multimodal, so each model is estimated
from several random starts and the solution with the highest likelihood is
retained. The number of starts is set by `n_starts`, which, like every other
estimation argument, applies identically to all candidates. Three starts per
model are used here to limit computation; applied analyses should use at
least ten, and a grid is re-estimated in its entirety when more starts are
required, so that every candidate has the same opportunity to reach its
maximum. The argument `seed` makes the starts reproducible. When many starts
are used, a candidate with more profiles than the data support can reach a
degenerate solution in which one profile collapses on a single observation
with every variance at its lower bound; its likelihood, and hence its
criteria, then depend on `min_variance` rather than on the data.
`boundary = "exclude"` sets such starts aside for every candidate (see
*Diagnostics of the estimation*). A profile can also be spurious without
reaching the bound, when a few nearly coincident observations give it
variances close to zero (McLachlan and Peel, 2000, section 3.10). A profile
with fewer effective members than its own means and variances is therefore
reported by a `latents_thin_profiles` warning. The argument
`search = "emEM"` screens five times `n_starts` starts by a short EM run each
and continues the best `n_starts` to convergence (Biernacki, Celeux and
Govaert, 2003); it reaches the highest maximum more often than the default
search, and for the same reason also reaches spurious maxima more often.

```{r enumerate}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models
```

```{r models-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_failed <- with(candidates, sum(is.na(log_likelihood)))
best <- get_results(models, "best")
pick <- function(name, convention_name) {
  with(subset(best, criterion == name & convention %in% convention_name),
       candidate)
}
bic_groups_pick <- pick("bic", "groups")
bic_individual_pick <- pick("bic", "individuals")
icl_groups_pick <- pick("icl", "groups")
awe_groups_pick <- pick("awe", "groups")
aic_pick <- with(subset(best, criterion == "aic"), candidate)
# The code below names these candidates; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(bic_groups_pick == "profiles4_groups3",
          icl_groups_pick == "profiles4_groups2",
          awe_groups_pick == "profiles3_groups2",
          aic_pick == "profiles6_groups4")
```

The result contains `r n_candidates` candidates. Each is named by its
numbers of profiles and group classes (`profiles4_groups3` denotes four
profiles and three group classes), and this name identifies the candidate in
all subsequent functions. The `r n_failed` candidates with a single profile
and more than one group class are not identified: group classes are defined
by differences in the distribution of profiles, and with a single profile no
such differences exist. These candidates are retained in the table together
with the error that terminated their estimation.

## The table of candidates

`as.data.frame()` returns one row per candidate.

```{r table}
as.data.frame(models)
```

The columns form the following groups.

| Columns | Content |
|---|---|
| `candidate`, `n_profiles`, `n_group_classes`, `model` | Identity of the candidate |
| `log_likelihood`, `n_parameters` | Fit and size |
| `aic`, `kic`, `bic_*`, `sabic_*`, `caic_*`, `awe_*`, `icl_*`, `clc_*` | Information criteria |
| `profile_entropy`, `group_entropy` | Relative entropy at each level |
| `avepp_min`, `avepp_max`, `avepp_mean`, `avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the profiles |
| `group_avepp_min`, `group_avepp_max`, `group_avepp_mean`, `group_avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the group classes |
| `converged`, `boundary`, `n_best_replicated`, `warnings`, `error` | Diagnostics of the estimation |

## Information criteria

An information criterion is the deviance, minus twice the maximized
log-likelihood, plus a penalty for the estimated parameters; lower values
indicate a more favourable balance of fit and complexity. In a two-level
model the penalty of several criteria depends on the sample size. Criteria
with the suffix `_groups` treat the `r n_students` students as the
independent units, and criteria with the suffix `_individual` the
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments (Lukočienė, Varriale and
Vermunt, 2010). A single convention should be used throughout an analysis.

The candidate that minimizes each criterion:

```{r best}
get_results(models, "best")
```

The criteria do not agree. With students as the units, the Bayesian
information criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) is minimized by
`r bic_groups_pick`, the integrated completed likelihood (ICL; Biernacki,
Celeux and Govaert, 2000) by `r icl_groups_pick` and the approximate weight
of evidence (AWE; Banfield and Raftery, 1993) by `r awe_groups_pick`. With
enrolments as the units, BIC is minimized by `r bic_individual_pick`. The
Akaike information criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974) is minimized by
`r aic_pick`, the largest candidate, because its weak penalty leaves it
decreasing over the entire range. ICL and AWE penalize classification
uncertainty in addition to the number of parameters and therefore favour
fewer, better separated classes.

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, with one line per
number of group classes and the minimum of each criterion circled.

```{r plot-criteria, fig.height = 5}
plot_enumeration(models)
```

A minimum at the largest number of profiles or group classes considered
indicates that the criterion is still decreasing at the boundary of the
grid, which should then be extended until the minimum is interior. Any
criterion can be plotted by name, and `what = "all"` plots all of them.

```{r plot-bic}
plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")
```

The clustering tree (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018) shows how the profiles divide
as their number increases: each profile of a model is linked to the profiles
of the next larger model that receive its observations. Each number of group
classes has its own tree, selected with `n_group_classes`; without it, every
tree is returned as a separate plot. The guide *Tree plot* covers the
comparison of solutions at one number of profiles and the tree of group
classes.

```{r plot-tree, fig.height = 6}
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)
```

## Change with each additional class

When a criterion decreases over the entire range, the magnitude of each
decrease constitutes the evidence. For each candidate, the table reports the
decrease in BIC relative to the candidate with one profile fewer and the
same number of group classes, and relative to the candidate with one group
class fewer and the same number of profiles. A positive value indicates that
the additional class lowered the criterion. Another criterion is selected
with `using`.

```{r deltas}
get_results(models, "deltas")
```

```{r deltas-values, include = FALSE}
deltas <- get_results(models, "deltas")
delta_of <- function(name) {
  with(subset(deltas, candidate == name), round(delta_profile))
}
step_3 <- delta_of("profiles3_groups3")
step_4 <- delta_of("profiles4_groups3")
step_5 <- delta_of("profiles5_groups3")
stopifnot(step_3 > 0, step_4 > 0, step_5 < 0)
```

With three group classes, a third profile lowers BIC by
`r format(step_3, big.mark = ",")` and a fourth by
`r format(step_4, big.mark = ",")`, whereas a fifth raises it by
`r format(-step_5, big.mark = ",")`, which the table reports as a negative
decrease. The decreases are plotted in both directions, along the number of
profiles (left) and along the number of group classes (right).

```{r plot-deltas, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")
```

The knee summary rescales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and
identifies the candidate at the greatest perpendicular distance below the
chord joining the first and last points. The rule follows the geometric
definition of Kneedle (Satopää et al., 2011) without its smoothing and
sensitivity threshold. A nearly linear curve yields a small maximum
distance, so the reported distance indicates the strength of the bend as
well as its location. Knees are computed along the number of profiles for
each number of group classes, along the number of group classes for each
number of profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of
parameters.

```{r knees}
get_results(models, "knees")
```

```{r knee-values, include = FALSE}
knees <- get_results(models, "knees")
profile_line <- subset(knees, direction == "profiles" &
                         line == "3 group classes")
knee_along_profiles <- with(profile_line, knee_candidate)
knee_without_largest <- with(profile_line, knee_without_largest)
knee_along_groups <- with(subset(knees, direction == "group_classes" &
                                   line == "4 profiles"), knee_candidate)
```

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is
`r knee_along_profiles`. Because the chord terminates at the largest
candidate, the knee depends on the range of the grid; with the largest
candidate omitted it is `r knee_without_largest`, as recorded in the
columns `stable` and `note`. Along the number of group classes with four
profiles, the knee is `r knee_along_groups`.

The criterion across all candidates simultaneously, expressed as the
distance of each from the minimum:

```{r heatmap}
plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")
```

## Classification quality

Each observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class.
Relative entropy (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) summarizes these probabilities
over all observations; it equals 0 when every observation is equally likely
to belong to every class and 1 when every observation is assigned to one
class with certainty. The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class
is the mean posterior probability of that class among the observations
modally assigned to it (Nagin, 2005). Values of at least 0.7 to 0.8 are
conventionally regarded as indicating adequate separation. The table of
candidates reports the minimum, maximum and mean AvePP at each level and the
number of classes below a cutoff, 0.8 by default, which is set with
`cutoff`.

```{r quality}
plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")
```

The AvePP of every class of every candidate, together with its size and the
relative entropy of its level:

```{r classification}
get_results(models, "classification")
```

```{r quality-values, include = FALSE}
chosen_row <- subset(candidates, candidate == bic_groups_pick)
profile_entropy_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(profile_entropy, 2))
group_entropy_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(group_entropy, 2))
avepp_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(avepp_min, 2))
group_avepp_chosen <- with(chosen_row, round(group_avepp_min, 2))
```

For `r bic_groups_pick`, the relative entropy is
`r profile_entropy_chosen` for the profiles and `r group_entropy_chosen` for
the group classes; the minimum AvePP is `r avepp_chosen` among the profiles
and `r group_avepp_chosen` among the group classes.

## Diagnostics of the estimation

A maximum reached from several random starts is more credible than one
reached once, since a single start may terminate at a local maximum. An
estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, such as a variance at its
lower bound, indicates a model too complex for the data, and a class
containing a very small proportion of the observations is difficult to
interpret and to replicate. The following plots report these diagnostics
for every candidate.

```{r trust}
plot_selection(models, what = "trust")
```

```{r smallest}
plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")
```

`plot_selection(models)` displays all plots relevant to the
choice of the number of classes jointly.

A candidate on a boundary whose smallest profile holds about one observation
is a degenerate solution, not a profile: a Gaussian profile centred on one
observation raises the likelihood without limit as its variances shrink, so
the reported likelihood is fixed by `min_variance`. The default,
`boundary = "allow"`, reports it, as Mplus does, with a warning.
`boundary = "exclude"` retains for each candidate the best start with no
variance at its lower bound, and is advisable when many starts are used,
since each additional start increases the chance of reaching such a
solution. Categorical indicators are unaffected.

```{r exclude, eval = FALSE}
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:5, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 200,
                            boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)
```

## Comparing candidates

`compare_models()` tabulates selected candidates side by side. Candidates
are specified by name, by their numbers of classes, or by a number of
profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from
the minimum among the compared candidates and the BIC weight,
`exp(-delta_bic / 2)` normalized to sum to one, which approximates the
posterior probability of each candidate under equal prior probabilities
(Wagenmakers and Farrell, 2004).

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

```{r compare-names}
compare_models(models, bic_groups_pick, icl_groups_pick, awe_groups_pick)
```

The same candidates specified by their numbers of classes, with labels:

```{r compare-counts}
compare_models(models, bic = c(4, 3), icl = c(4, 2), awe = c(3, 2))
```

All candidates with four profiles, which isolates the contribution of the
group classes:

```{r compare-select}
comparison <- compare_models(models, n_profiles = 4)
comparison
plot(comparison)
```

The comparison retains the fitted models. `get_results()` returns the AvePP
of every class of every compared model, and `get_candidate()` the model
underlying a row.

```{r compare-classification}
get_results(comparison, "classification")
```

## Analysis of the chosen candidate

The analysis proceeds with `r bic_groups_pick`, the candidate that minimizes
BIC with students as the units. It is extracted by name with
`get_candidate()`; specifying the numbers of classes, as in
`get_candidate(models, 4, 3)`, returns the same model.

```{r chosen}
chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
```

`chosen` is an object of the class returned by `multilpa()`. Its summary
reports the estimates with their standard errors.

```{r chosen-summary}
summary(chosen)
```

The profiles are displayed as their means on the five indicators.

```{r chosen-profiles}
plot_profiles(chosen)
```

Each group class has its own distribution over the four profiles.

```{r chosen-prevalence}
plot_prevalence(chosen)
```

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

```{r chosen-diagnostics}
diagnostics(chosen)
```

```{r chosen-diagnostic-plots, fig.height = 7}
plot_diagnostics(chosen)
```

With two or more group classes, the four views for the enrolments in their
profiles are followed by the same views for the students in their group
classes. Because a student is classified from all of their enrolments
jointly, the group classes are typically far better separated than the
profiles. A single view is selected with `what`, for example
`plot_diagnostics(chosen, what = "group_posteriors")`.

Each enrolment with its modal profile, the group class of its student and
its posterior probabilities:

```{r chosen-assignments}
head(get_results(chosen, "assignments", data = course_engagement))
```

The profiles can be related to external variables. The mean of
`previous_grade` in each profile is estimated with `three_step()`, which
corrects for classification error by the BCH method (Bolck, Croon and
Hagenaars, 2004; Vermunt, 2010).

```{r chosen-outcome}
three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
```

## Testing neighbouring candidates

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) compares two
candidates that differ by one class. Data sets are simulated from the
smaller candidate and both candidates are re-estimated on each. With `B`
simulated data sets, of which `b` yield a likelihood ratio at least as large
as the observed one, the p-value is `(b + 1) / (B + 1)` (Davison and
Hinkley, 1997); the additional count includes the observed statistic and
precludes a p-value of zero from a finite simulation. The p-value is
withheld unless every replicate satisfies the estimation checks. The test
below compares three and four profiles with three group classes. Nineteen
simulated data sets keep the example brief; the smallest attainable p-value
is then 1/20 = 0.05, and applied analyses should use at least 99.

```{r blrt}
smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
plot(test)
```

## Other model types

### Latent class models

```{r lca-values, include = FALSE}
n_reports <- nrow(student_esm)
```

`student_esm` contains `r format(n_reports, big.mark = ",")` momentary
reports from students, with eight activities recorded as present or absent.
Declaring the indicators in `categorical` makes every candidate a latent
class model, and the candidates are named with `classes` in place of
`profiles`.

```{r lca}
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
lca_models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:2,
                                categorical = activities, n_starts = 5,
                                seed = 1)
lca_models
plot_selection(lca_models, what = "diagnostics")
compare_models(lca_models, n_profiles = 3)
```

```{r lca-check, include = FALSE}
lca_row <- subset(as.data.frame(lca_models), candidate == "classes3_groups2")
lca_entropy <- with(lca_row, round(profile_entropy, 2))
lca_avepp <- with(lca_row, round(avepp_min, 2))
lca_lowest <- with(subset(get_results(compare_models(lca_models, n_profiles = 3),
                                     "comparison"), delta_bic == min(delta_bic)),
                   model)
stopifnot(lca_entropy < 0.6, lca_avepp < 0.7, lca_lowest == "classes3_groups2")
```

Among the three-class models, the model with two group classes has the
lower BIC. Its relative entropy is `r lca_entropy`, and its least distinct
class has an AvePP of `r lca_avepp`. The classes of this model overlap
substantially, which limits their substantive interpretation.

### Single-level models

Observations without a grouping structure are modelled with
`enumerate_lpa()` for continuous indicators and `enumerate_lca()` for
categorical indicators. The candidates are named by their numbers of
profiles or classes alone.

```{r single}
srl_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                                   "self_efficacy", "self_regulation",
                                   "test_anxiety"),
                            n_profiles = 1:8, model = "VVI", n_starts = 10,
                            seed = 1)
srl_models
compare_models(srl_models, "profiles5", "profiles6", "profiles7")
plot_selection(srl_models, what = "deltas")
```

```{r single-check, include = FALSE}
srl_bic <- with(subset(get_results(srl_models, "best"),
                       criterion == "bic" & convention == "groups"),
                candidate)
eight_on_boundary <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models),
                                 candidate == "profiles8"), boundary)
warned <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), nzchar(warnings)), candidate)
thin <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), grepl("members for", warnings)),
             candidate)
stopifnot(srl_bic == "profiles6", isTRUE(eight_on_boundary),
          identical(warned, c("profiles6", "profiles7", "profiles8")),
          identical(thin, warned))
```

BIC is minimized by `r srl_bic`. The six- and seven-profile candidates each
contain a profile of about ten observations, about 3% of the sample, too few
to determine its own ten means and variances, and the enumeration reports
this with a `latents_thin_profiles` warning; such a profile may be a
spurious maximum, and the BIC choice should be weighed against the
five-profile candidate, which `compare_models()` shows beside it. The
eight-profile candidate has a variance at its lower bound and a nearly empty
profile, which marks the limit of what `r nrow(srl)` observations can
support. Every warning issued during the enumeration is retained in the
`warnings` column of the table.

### Missing values and scaled indicators

Two arguments alter the data to which the candidates are fitted and, like
`n_starts`, apply to all candidates. With `missing = "fiml"`, rows with some
indicators missing contribute through the indicators observed (full
information maximum likelihood); rows with every indicator missing are
excluded from the individual sample size, entropy and AvePP, since they
carry no information on class membership. `centering` subtracts and
`scaling` divides by a mean or standard deviation computed over the sample
(`"grand"`) or within each group (`"person"`); combined, they yield grand
or within-person z-scores. Information criteria are comparable only among
candidates fitted under the same settings. [Model
selection](model-selection.html) describes both with examples.

### Multiple covariance structures

Specifying several structures in `model` multiplies the candidates, and the
structure is appended to each name. Because the numbers of classes then
match several candidates, a candidate must be specified by its full name.

```{r crossed}
crossed_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies",
                                       "intrinsic_value", "self_efficacy",
                                       "self_regulation", "test_anxiety"),
                                n_profiles = 2:4, model = c("VVI", "EEE"),
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
crossed_models
compare_models(crossed_models, "profiles3_VVI", "profiles3_EEE")
```

### Latent transition models

With `time`, every candidate is a latent transition model over the
occasions, here the order of each student's enrolments in `sequence`. The
six-profile model requires more than the default 1,000 EM iterations to meet
the convergence tolerance, so `max_iter` is increased.

```{r transitions}
transition_models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                                       time = "sequence", n_profiles = 2:6,
                                       n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 3,
                                       max_iter = 2000, seed = 1)
transition_models
compare_models(transition_models)
```

```{r transitions-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(all(as.data.frame(transition_models)$converged))
```
